summary:
Perm Krai is a federal subject of Russia and stands under the national framework set out in the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025; assessment updated 11 June 2025): same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and no specific legal protections apply. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law barring gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed.

The expanded 'propaganda' law criminalises public expression that 'justifies' gender transition. It carries administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to four years in prison. Foreigners who breach these statutes face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings to LGBT travellers state this risk directly; the US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel.

The Supreme Court of Russia designated the 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation in 2023. Participating carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment and organising carries 6 to 10 years. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 convictions for extremism tied to that designation as of 30 June 2025. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation; courts sentenced two of them to prison and one detainee died by suicide in pretrial detention.

Displaying banned symbols is prosecuted under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses. In the same period 81 people were found guilty across 98 such cases, and participants in the designated movement face up to 12 years in prison. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people across Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions.

Enforcement volume has risen alongside severity. Cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow: about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two further venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented alongside the statutory penalties. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed 'Ada', a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
tangentialFactors:
The UK Home Office country policy note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including in the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. A Russian man detained in December 2024 on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was reported by the Associated Press to have been found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Independent media coverage indicates a sustained climate rather than a single operation. The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, and quoted a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as a second-class citizen after the extremist designation.

Survey findings cited in the UK Home Office note show respondents in the Volga area, the federal district containing Perm Krai, reported being more closeted toward relatives than the whole-study sample, indicating a higher degree of concealment in family settings than the national pattern.
localsOnly:
Residents of Perm Krai have no lawful route to legal gender recognition or gender-affirming care, since the 2023 legislation removed both across Russia, and no mechanism for same-sex marriage exists. No specific legal protections against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity apply.

Exposure to the anti-LGBT+ legal regime is measurable rather than theoretical: at least 139 people in Russia were impacted between 2022 and 2024 through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions, and 101 extremism convictions tied to the 2023 designation had been issued by 30 June 2025. Administrative liability under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses reached 81 people across 98 cases between January 2024 and June 2025 for displaying banned symbols.

Concealment within families runs higher in the Volga area than in the study sample overall, which affects how residents manage relationships with relatives as well as contact with the authorities.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Perm Krai-specific enforcement records, regional prosecutions or local police directives are contained in the sourced material. The frequency with which the national statutes have been applied inside Perm Krai itself is unresolved.

The documented conversion-therapy detention concerns a centre near Novosibirsk; whether comparable private coercion operates in Perm Krai is not sourced either way.

Whether Perm Krai has adopted regional bylaws, administrative rules or policing practices supplementing the federal framework is not addressed by the available sources and remains unresolved.

The number of fatalities in custody linked to the extremist designation is incomplete: one suicide in pretrial detention is recorded between January 2024 and June 2025, and a separate death was reported in December 2024, but the total is not established.
